doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

title: Chicago and Blood, Sweat & Tears versus straight-ahead jazz
summary: He liked rock-influenced bands but was drawn to straight-ahead jazz because the soloists were unleashed there.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well said. When I was at Fredonia, this was late 60s, early 70s, we used to put on Blood, Sweat & Tears and Chicago, and for our age group at that time, like oh man, I want to do that.
Did you ever have that — did you have a band or a — for you was it more the big bands?

That was my first inspiration, although I did listen to groups like that. I had Chicago records and Blood, Sweat & Tears records and things like that, and I got to work with Blood, Sweat & Tears when I moved to New York, a few times. But it was more the straight-ahead jazz that inspired me. And I’m not sure why that was but it was. I mean I liked all the more modern stuff. I listened to the Maynard Ferguson albums in the 70s when he was doing all the rock stuff and it was — a lot of that stuff was very interesting to me and I thought it was great. But I think it was because I wanted to be an improviser and all the great improvisers played over straight-ahead music. All the people I wanted to sound like played over straight-ahead music at the time. So I just got more and more into that. And I realized that there was more and more to that. I mean obviously Blood, Sweat
& Tears had a lot of great jazz harmony, as did Chicago. But as far as the soloists go, they weren’t unleashed as much as they were in jazz.
Right. It’s a shame sometimes when you hear Blood, Sweat & Tears on like the oldies station or whatever, they always snip out those middle parts with the —
The extended, yeah. It’s sad to hear.
